'''Bell Masayuki Shimada''' ({{langx|ja|島田 正雪}},<ref>[https://hojishinbun.hoover.org/?a=d&d=csp19580607-01.1.3&srpos=1&e=-------ja-10--1--img-%E5%B3%B6%E7%94%B0%E3%83%99%E3%83%AB-------- シカゴ新報 = Chicago Shimpo 1958.06.07: Page 3]</ref> January 17, 1922 - June 2, 1958) was an American [[Fisheries science|fisheries scientist]]. He is noted for his study during the 1950s of [[tuna]] stocks in the [[Tropics|tropical]] [[Pacific Ocean]] and its important effect on the development of the post-[[World War II]] tuna [[fishery]] on the [[United States West Coast]].<ref name=preserve>[http://preserveamerica.noaa.gov/week06/shimada_bio.html preserveamerica.noaa.gov Bell Masayuki Shimada (1922-1958)]</ref><ref name=nvc>{{Cite web |url=https://www.nvcfoundation.org/newsletter/2008/12/noaa-honors-nisei-with-launch-of-fisheries-vessel-bell-m-shimada/ |title=nvcfoundation.org "NOAA Honors Nisei with Launch of Fisheries Vessel 'Bell M. Shimada,'" Japanese American Veterans Association, December 2008, Volume 58, Issue 11. |access-date=2016-12-21 |archive-date=2017-05-10 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170510181649/https://www.nvcfoundation.org/newsletter/2008/12/noaa-honors-nisei-with-launch-of-fisheries-vessel-bell-m-shimada/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

==Biography==

===Early life===
Shimada was born in [[Seattle, Washington]], on January 17, 1922, to [[Japanese people|Japanese]] immigrant parents.<ref name=preserve/> As a boy, he demonstrated an aptitude for mathematics and science. After graduating from [[Franklin High School (Seattle)|Franklin High School]], he attended the [[University of Washington]], where he studied at the School of [[Fishery|Fisheries]].<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/>

The [[United States]] entered [[World War II]] with the [[Japanese attack on Pearl Harbor]] in December 1941. Early in the war, concerns arose in the United States that [[Japanese-American]]s might sympathize with [[Japan]], leading to a program of  [[Internment of Japanese Americans|internment of Japanese-Americans]] which involved "evacuating" them involuntarily from the [[United States West Coast]] and incarcerating them in inland [[concentration camp]]s. This interrupted Shimada's studies when he was "evacuated" on April 27, 1942.<ref name=preserve/> He was incarcerated at [[Minidoka National Historic Site|Minidoka]] in [[Idaho]] on April 29, 1942.<ref name=nvc/><ref name=archives>{{cite web | title=Japanese American Internee Data File: Masauki [sic] Shimada|url=https://aad.archives.gov/aad/record-detail.jsp?dt=3099&mtch=3&tf=F&q=Masauki&bc=&rpp=10&pg=1&rid=78250&rlst=78250,11881,108687|publisher=[[National Archives and Records Administration]]| accessdate=August 18, 2019}}</ref>

===Military service===
In May 1943, Shimada was permitted to leave the camp and enlist in the [[United States Army]] as an [[infantry]]man<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/> in the [[442nd Infantry Regiment (United States)|442nd]] [[Regimental Combat Team]].<ref name=nvc/> After [[Recruit training|basic training]] at [[Camp Shelby]] in [[Hattiesburg, Mississippi|Hattiesburg]], [[Mississippi]], he was selected for [[Japanese language]] and [[military intelligence]] collection training at [[Camp Savage]] in [[Savage, Minnesota|Savage]], [[Minnesota]]. In April 1944, he was transferred to the [[United States Army Air Forces]] and received three months of [[Air intelligence officer|air intelligence]] training in [[Orlando, Florida|Orlando]], [[Florida]]. He then was transferred to [[Honolulu, Hawaii|Honolulu]], [[Hawaii]], where he served as a [[Translation|translator]] and [[Language interpretation|interpreter]] until May 1945, when he was transferred to [[Guam]], where he served as a [[radio]] traffic monitor until the [[surrender of Japan]] on August 15, 1945.<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/>

In August 1945, Shimada moved to U.S. Army Air Forces headquarters in [[Tokyo]] to take part in the [[occupation of Japan]]. He collected and synthesized economic and infrastructure data on the effects of the [[strategic bombing]] of Japan until he was discharged from the military in February 1946.<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/>

===Fisheries science career===
[[File:Bell Shimada and Fred Cleaver and examining skipjack.jpg|thumb|Bell M. Shimada (left) and Fred Cleaver examining skipjack tuna, circa 1951]]
[[File:Bell M. Shimada.jpg|thumb|Bell M. Shimada, circa 1957]]

====Research for Supreme Commander for the Allied Forces====
Remaining in Japan, Shimada accepted a civilian position as a fisheries biologist in the Natural Resources Section on the staff of the [[Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers]] (SCAP). His duties involved researching and analyzing Japanese fisheries activities and compiling and collating data on them. He played a major role in drafting SCAP directives to the [[Government of Japan|Japanese government]], particularly on [[whaling]], and his first professional publication, ''Japanese Whaling in the [[Bonin Islands]] Area'' ([[United States Fish and Wildlife Service]], Fishery Leaflet No. 248), published in 1947, was based on his studies and reports on whaling while he was in Japan.<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/>

Leaving Japan in December 1946, Shimada returned to the University of Washington to resume his studies at the College of Fisheries. He also worked as a laboratory technician for the School of Fisheries and maintained the School's [[ichthyology]] collection. After graduating ''[[cum laude]]'' on December 20, 1947, and receiving his [[bachelor's degree]], he remained at the School of Fisheries to pursue [[postgraduate studies]], during which he worked as a laboratory assistant maintaining [[aquaculture]] facilities for the [[United States Atomic Energy Commission|Atomic Energy Commission]]. In September 1948, he began his career with the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service, accepting a position in its Bureau of Fisheries.<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/>

====Pacific Ocean Fisheries Investigations====
Shimada graduated from the University of Washington School of Fisheries postgraduate program with a [[Master of Science]] in Fisheries in December 1948, and the same month moved to Honolulu to work for the Fish and Wildlife Service's new Pacific Ocean Fishery Investigations (POFI) office.<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/> Tuna stocks in the [[Pacific Ocean]] had come under increasing pressure since the end of World War II, and the Fish and Wildlife Service had created POFI to study the tuna fishery in the [[equator]]ial Pacific. POFI's first director, the influential fisheries scientist [[Oscar Elton Sette]], arrived in Honolulu to take charge of POFI in 1949. Sette has been credited with pioneering modern fisheries science by integrating the biological study of fish and their life cycles and populations with [[oceanography]] and [[meteorology]] to develop an overall understanding not only of the biology of the fish themselves but also of the influence of the physical environment on fisheries and fluctuations in their abundance from year to year.<ref name=powell>{{Cite web |url=http://www.aifrb.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/05/AIFRB-Biographies-web.pdf |title=Powell, Patricia, ''Fishery Bulletin'', National Marine Fisheries Service, Volume 70, Number 3, July 1972, pages 525-535, in aifrb.org AIFRB-Biographies-web.pdf |access-date=2016-12-21 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220174404/http://www.aifrb.org/wp-content/uploads/2011/05/AIFRB-Biographies-web.pdf |archive-date=2016-12-20 |url-status=dead }}</ref><ref name=kendall>{{Cite web |url=http://acoustics.washington.edu/fis437/resources/Week%201/Kendall%26Duker1998.pdf |title=Kendall, Arthur W., Jr., and Gary J. Duker, "The development of recruitment fisheries oceanography in the United States," ''Fisheries Oceanography'' 7:2, pp. 69-88, 1998. |access-date=2016-12-21 |archive-date=2016-12-20 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20161220194026/http://acoustics.washington.edu/fis437/resources/Week%201/Kendall%26Duker1998.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> Sette organized and directed POFI according to this vision.<ref name=powell/><ref name=kendall/>

Under Sette's guidance, Shimada worked with many accomplished fisheries scientists and oceanographers while at POFI, including [[Wilbert McLeod Chapman|Wilbert McLeod "Wib" Chapman]], [[Roger Revelle]], [[Milner Baily Schaefer|Milner Baily "Benny" Schaefer]], and Sette himself, as well as young scientists who would become notable in their fields as their careers progressed, such as [[Townsend Cromwell]], [[Fred Cleaver]], [[Warren Wooster]], [[Alan Tubbs]], [[William Aron]], [[Gerald Howard (scientist)|Gerald Howard]], [[Richard Hennemuth]], [[Howard Yoshida]], and [[Tom Hida]].<ref name=preserve/> The Fish and Wildlife Service assigned two [[research ship]]s to support POFI, and Shimada served as a seagoing biologist, in charge of shipboard science watches and research.<ref name=preserve/>

Shimada also took postgraduate courses while in Honolulu and began work on his [[Doctor of Philosophy|Ph.D.]]<ref name=preserve/> He left POFI in January 1951 and spent the rest of the year in Seattle taking doctoral courses at the School of Fisheries at the University of Washington.<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/>

====Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission====
In February 1952, Shimada was assigned to the [[Inter-American Tropical Tuna Commission]] (IATTC),<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/> which was collocated with the [[Scripps Institution of Oceanography]] and the Fish and Wildlife Service Bureau of Fisheries laboratory in [[La Jolla, California|La Jolla]], [[California]], and he cooperated professionally with those institutions on matters of mutual interest, sharing scientific ideas and manpower and cooperating in research. Working with Milner "Benny" Schaefer and Gerald Howard, Shimada conducted the tuna fishery research for which he is best known during his time with the IATTC and achieved national and international recognition when he began to publish his research on tuna spawning, distribution, and feeding patterns.<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/> He received his doctorate from the University of Washington School of Fisheries in 1956,<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/> and rose rapidly within the IATTC, serving as the IATTC's Senior Scientist from 1956 to 1958.  Both at POFI and at IATTC, Shimada worked frequently with [[Townsend Cromwell]], a physical oceanographer interested in [[ocean current]]s, on research into the distribution of tuna in the Pacific Ocean. Their cooperative work, following the principles of fisheries oceanography Sette, Shimada, Cromwell, and other members of Sette's team had pioneered at POFI, combined Cromwell's insights into the forces such as temperature gradients that drive currents with Shimada's findings regarding the availability of forage for the tunas, leading to useful research results for both men.<ref name=preserve/>

In 1957, Shimada and Cromwell worked together on the distribution of tuna throughout the Pacific Ocean,<ref name=nvc/> including a research ship cruise off [[Mexico]]'s [[Clarion Island]] as part of a project for the IATTC known as the Island Current Study.<ref name=preserve/> Plans called for Shimada and Cromwell to make one more cruise to Clarion Island in 1958 aboard the Scripps Institution research ship ''Horizon'' to continue their research there before Shimada left the IATTC to take up a position as the first director of the Fish and Wildlife Service Bureau of Commercial Fisheries' new Eastern Pacific Tuna Investigations office in July 1958.<ref name=preserve/>

===Death===

Making their way to [[Acapulco]], Mexico, to join their research team for the 1958 Clarion Island cruise, Shimada and Cromwell boarded [[Aeronaves de México]] [[Aeronaves de México Flight 111]], a [[Lockheed L-749 Constellation|Lockheed L-749A Constellation]], in [[Guadalajara]], Mexico, on June 2, 1958, for a flight to [[Mexico City]]. Shortly after takeoff, the airliner crashed into La Latilla Mountain, only 16 kilometers (10 miles) from [[Guadalajara Airport]], killing all 45 people on board in what at the time was Mexico's deadliest aviation accident.<ref name=preserve/><ref name=nvc/><ref>[https://aviation-safety.net/database/record.php?id=19580602-1 Aviation Safety Network Accident Description]</ref>

==Personal life==

[[File:Allen and Julie Shimada.jpg|thumb|Allen and Julie Shimada, at the commissioning ceremony for the ship named for their father, [[NOAAS Bell M. Shimada (R 227)|NOAAS ''Bell M. Shimada'' (R 227)]], in 2010.]]

While working with POFI in Hawaii between 1948 and 1952, Shimada met and married the former Rae M. Shimojima,<ref name=preserve/> who was working as Sette's secretary at the time.<ref name=nvc/> They had a son, Allen, born in 1954, and a daughter, Julie, born in 1957.<ref name=preserve/> Allen Shimada later became a fisheries scientist with the [[National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration]]'s [[National Marine Fisheries Service]].<ref name=noaasshimada>[http://www.noaanews.noaa.gov/stories2010/20100825_shimada.html .noaanews.noaa.gov "NOAA Commissions New Research Ship Bell M. Shimada," 25 August 2010.]</ref>

==Commemoration==
[[File:NOAA Ship Bell M Shimada underway.jpg|300px|thumb|right|[[NOAAS Bell M. Shimada (R 227)|NOAAS ''Bell M. Shimada'' (R 227)]]]]
Although Shimada died at the age of 36 and his fisheries science career lasted only 12 years, at the time of his death the fisheries science community already viewed his contributions as so significant to both the scientific understanding of the Pacific tuna fishery and to the post-World War II development of that fishery on the U.S. West Coast that the Proceedings from the Symposium on "The Changing Pacific Ocean in 1957 and 1958" were dedicated to him,<ref name=preserve/><ref name=symposium>{{Cite web |url=http://www.calcofi.org/publications/calcofireports/v07/Vol_07_Symposium_Front_Pieces.pdf |title="Dedication" in Sette, Oscar Elton, and John D. Isaacs, eds., Part II: Symposium on "The Changing Pacific Ocean in 1957 and 1958," Rancho Santa Fe, California, June 2-4, 1958. |access-date=2016-12-21 |archive-date=2019-08-03 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190803032754/http://www.calcofi.org/publications/calcofireports/v07/Vol_07_Symposium_Front_Pieces.pdf |url-status=dead }}</ref> as well as to Townsend Cromwell.<ref name=symposium/> The dedication read:

{{blockquote|This Symposium is dedicated to Townsend Cromwell and Bell M. Shimada, associates in research of many of the participants in this Symposium, who lost their lives, June 2, 1958, in an airplane crash near Guadalajara, Mexico, while en route to join the research vessel ''Horizon'' to make further observations on the changing conditions in 1958."<ref name=symposium/>}}

The [[Shimada Seamount]] in the Pacific Ocean southwest of [[Baja California]] at {{coord|16|52|N|117|31|W|name=Shimada Seamount}} is named for Shimada.<ref name=preserve/><ref>[https://earthref.org/SC/SMNT-169N-1175W/ earthref.org Seamount Catalog: Shimada Seamount]</ref>

The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration [[research ship]] [[NOAAS Bell M. Shimada (R 227)|NOAAS ''Bell M. Shimada'' (R 227)]] is named in honor of Shimada.<ref name=nvc/><ref name=noaasshimada/>  A team of students from [[Marina High School (Marina, California)|Marina High School]] in [[Marina, California|Marina]], California, that suggested the name won a regional NOAA contest to name the vessel.<ref name=nvc/><ref name=noaasshimada/> In a speech at the ship's [[Ceremonial ship launching|launching ceremony]] on September 26, 2008, Shimada's daughter Julie said, "I hope the ''Bell M. Shimada'' is a lasting testament that no life is too short, no career too brief, no contribution too small, to make a difference."<ref name=nvc/> The ship was [[Ship commissioning|commissioned]] into the [[NOAA ships and aircraft|NOAA fleet]] on August 25, 2010.<ref name=noaasshimada/>
